gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Starlink Mini's own input is rated 12–48 V at 60 W (25–40 W average). That means Starlink's '100 W, 20 V/5 A minimum' USB-C rule is about getting 5 A at 20 V, not about the dish needing 100 W. The extra 40 W on a '140 W' port only comes at 28 V (USB PD 3.1 EPR), which does nothing for the Mini. Some power stations also have a USB-C port that cannot run the Mini at all: on the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, USB-C1 shares a 20 W total with USB-A.
standout_why: I compared against Starlink's help pages that ChatGPT cited (a7fe6525 'How can I power my Starlink Mini?' and fba85643 'What USB power rating do I need'), the Mini accessories guide PDF (result 7/14) and the ctmods 'starlink mini usb-c pd requirements' post that ranks for this query. The help-center articles load with JavaScript and returned only the word 'Starlink', even through a text proxy, so I could not read their bodies. Search results show they repeat the 100 W / 20 V-5 A rule. The accessories guide states '100W (20V/5A) power source' and that the cable won't charge phones, but gives no input rating or draw. ctmods repeats 100 W, 20 V/5 A and notes that 100 W doesn't guarantee uptime. It doesn't mention 60 W input or 28 V vs 20 V. ChatGPT's answer mentions 20 V/5 A on a 140 W charger and 'single port vs total', but it calls 100 W a startup/peak need, which contradicts the 60 W input rating. It also never says which port on a given power station qualifies. Risk: result 12 ('Starlink Mini: Specifications and Installation') may list the 60 W input rating, and I could not render it to check.
decides: The table's USB-C column should read 'has a 20 V/5 A port: yes/no (which port)', not the headline port wattage. A 140 W port gives the Mini no more than a 100 W port does, so the extra watts above 100 shouldn't count in a product's favour. Pick the power station or power bank by usable Wh and a single 20 V/5 A port. For the Anker C1000 Gen 2, the page must say to use USB-C2 (20 V 5 A listed), not USB-C1 (20 W shared with USB-A). The page's runtime math should use 25–40 W (Starlink's average) and treat 60 W as the most the dish can draw, not 100 W. Our current page uses 20–40 W, and 20 W is below Starlink's stated average range.

findings.label: Input rating (dish)
findings.note: Read through the r.jina.ai text renderer. Verbatim row: 'Input Rating 12-48V 60W'. The PDF metadata shows it was published 28 May 2026.

findings.label: Average power consumption
findings.note: Verbatim: 'Power Consumption Average: 25-40W'. This is the figure to use for runtime: 1,024 Wh × 0.85 / 40 W ≈ 22 h; / 25 W ≈ 35 h. The 0.85 efficiency is an assumption, not a Starlink figure.

findings.label: USB PD requirement
findings.value: 100 W, 20 V/5 A minimum (with Starlink USB-C to Barrel Jack Cable)
findings.note: Verbatim: 'USB PD Requirement 100W, 20V/5A Minimum (with Starlink USB-C to Barrel Jack Cable Accessory)'. The same sheet rates the dish input at 60 W, so the 100 W is a rule for the source (a 5 A profile at 20 V), not what the dish draws.

findings.label: Source requirement and limitation
findings.value: Requires a 100 W (20 V/5 A) power source; designed only for powering the Mini, not for charging phones
findings.note: Read through the r.jina.ai renderer. The guide also says the Mini Car Adapter works with 12–24 V car outlets and comes with a Mini USB-C Cable.

findings.label: USB PD voltage behind 100 W vs 140 W
findings.value: 100 W = 20 V at 5 A (top of the standard range); 140 W needs the new 28 V fixed voltage
findings.note: Verbatim: 'Prior to this update, USB PD was limited to 100W using a solution based on 20V using USB Type-C cables rated at 5A' and 'New 28V, 36V, and 48V fixed voltages enable up to 140W, 180W and 240W'. The Mini asks for 20 V, so on a 140 W PD 3.1 port it gets at most 20 V × 5 A = 100 W. The extra 40 W exists only at 28 V.

findings.label: USB-C2 profiles
findings.note: Verbatim spec row; the page's '5V~ 3V' is a typo for 3 A. The listed 20 V 5 A profile meets Starlink's minimum, so this is the port to use for the Mini.

findings.label: USB-C1 limit
findings.value: USB-A and USB-C1 share 20 W max
findings.note: Verbatim: 'USB-A and USB-C1 Total 20W Max'. USB-C1 is far below 20 V/5 A, so it cannot run the Mini even though the unit is sold with '3 USB-C ports'. The page lists no separate row for USB-C3.

findings.label: Car outlet
findings.note: This is another way to power the Mini: Starlink's Mini Car Adapter is rated for 12–24 V outlets (accessories guide).

findings.label: USB-C PD
findings.value: USB-C port with PD 3.1, up to 140 W; 288 Wh; 600 W rated AC
findings.note: The Tech Specs block was empty. Copy said 'USB-C port with PD 3.1 protocol, delivering up to 140W output'. 140 W means 28 V; for the Mini it gives 20 V at up to 5 A = 100 W (USB-IF). Runtime: 288 Wh × 0.85 / 25–40 W ≈ 6.1–9.8 h. The 0.85 is assumed.
